items.title: Why a plaintext session token is dangerous
items.body:
The key is right: anyone who can read the Session table can impersonate every unexpired session, and hashing tokens at rest closes it. The cookie value *is* the database key: `Session.token` stores it as-is. Someone with read access (a leaked backup, an over-broad database user) can copy a token into their browser's cookie and the app will treat them as that user until it expires. If the table stored a hash (for example `sha256(token)`) and the app hashed the cookie at lookup, the stored values would be useless on their own.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Only the email; tokens are IP-bound": nothing binds a session to an IP.
- "Encrypt the cookie in the browser": the problem is what the server stores, not the browser.
- "Nothing, httpOnly cookies cannot be set by hand": httpOnly stops page scripts reading the cookie; it does not stop a person setting one in their own browser.

excerpts.quote: Anyone who can read the `Session` table can paste a token into a cookie and impersonate that user until it expires. Hashing the token before storage (and hashing the cookie value at lookup) would close this.

items.title: Goal: what saving "SECURITY" does to the existing tag
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal names a specific input (the tag "SECURITY") and an existing row (the tag "Security"), and asks what happens to that row.

The keyed Check follows the data: `slugify("SECURITY")` gives `security`, the same slug as the existing tag, so the upsert in `tagRepository.ts:22-26` finds it and runs `update: { name: "SECURITY" }`. Every entry tagged Security now shows the new casing.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The `findWorkspaceEntryById` check is about an over-broad single-entry read.
- The seeded-editor check is about what the editor's workspace lists.
- The `updateMutation` check is about saving a published entry.
Only the tag check mentions tags or slugs.

excerpts.quote: where: { slug: tag.slug }, update: { name: tag.name },
- **Goal:** Find what saving with the tag "SECURITY" does to the existing "Security" tag.

items.title: Goal: what happens to an empty slug field
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal is narrow: when the form's `slug` field is left empty, what slug does the entry get?

The keyed Check points at the one line that decides it: `slug: slugify(value.slug?.length ? value.slug : value.title)` in the save schema. If the slug has length, it is used; otherwise the title is slugified instead. So an empty slug falls back to the title.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The seeded-editor check answers the "what does the editor's workspace show" Goal.
- The `updateMutation.mutateAsync` check answers the "Save on a published entry" Goal.
- The `ReactMarkdown` check answers the raw-HTML Goal.
Only the schema line is about slugs at all.

excerpts.quote: - **Goal:** Find what happens to an empty `slug` field.

items.title: How login timing still reveals which emails exist
items.body:
The key is right: yes, by timing, because unknown emails skip the bcrypt compare. `loginWithEmail` first looks up the user. If there is none, it throws "Invalid email or password" immediately. If the user exists, it runs `verifyPassword`, a bcrypt compare that is slow on purpose, before throwing the same message. The text is identical, but the known-email case takes noticeably longer. By measuring response times, an attacker can tell which emails have accounts. The guide adds there is no rate limiting.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Through the status code": both failures throw the same `AuthenticationError`.
- "No, identical messages hide it": the guide says the message hides it in the body but timing does not.
- "Only with the Session table": timing needs nothing but the login endpoint.

excerpts.quote: if (!user) { throw new AuthenticationError("Invalid email or password"); } const isPasswordValid = await verifyPassword(password, user.passwordHash);
an unknown email returns at `authService.ts:21-23` without running bcrypt, while a known email pays for a 10-round compare.

items.title: Catching every error turns an outage into a 404
items.body:
The entry page wants two outcomes, show the entry or show not-found, and gets there with `.catch(() => null)` around the lookup. The service already signals a missing entry with its own `NotFoundError`, but the catch does not look at what it caught, so a dropped connection, a timeout or a bug in the mapper all become null and then `notFound()`. The reader sees a 404 page for an entry that exists, and nothing reaches the error boundary or the logs.

Catching only `NotFoundError` and rethrowing the rest keeps the two failure modes apart: a real 404 for missing content and the error page (plus a log line) for an outage.

- *The error page* is what the code would show without the catch.
- *A cached copy* does not exist for a page that reads cookies on each request.
- *A redirect* comes only from the session check, which already passed.

items.title: A Date in a shared type becomes a string on the wire
items.body:
On the server, `mapWorkspaceEntry` really does return Date objects, so the shared `WorkspaceEntry` type is true there. `apiOk` serializes with `NextResponse.json`, JSON has no date type, and the browser receives ISO strings. `apiClient` returns `payload.data as T`, a cast that converts nothing, so the client code still believes it holds a Date. The sort compiles, then `getTime` turns out to be undefined on a string and calling it throws a TypeError.

The existing components survive only because they wrap the value in `new Date(...)`. A separate wire type with `string` dates, or a parse step that revives them, would let the compiler catch this.

- *tsc fails* would need the client type to say string.
- *Revived dates* would need a reviver in `apiClient`.
- *NaN* would need a call that returns; this one throws.

items.title: Three layers of access control
items.body:
The auth guide opens with one sentence that organises everything else: there are three layers.

1. **Session.** Logging in creates a row in the `Session` table and sets a cookie. Read how a request finds its user, and what is stored in the row.
2. **Role threshold.** Route guards compare the user's role against a minimum (VIEWER is 1, EDITOR 2, ADMIN 3). Note the status each guard returns, and when.
3. **Ownership.** Inside the workspace, non-admins work on their own entries. Find every place that rule is applied, and what a request for someone else's entry gets back from each.

The guide's capability table shows, for each action, which layer enforces it and which roles pass. Read it slowly, then compare it with the code in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`.

Note also that the app is not multi-tenant: there are no separate organizations, just authors and their unpublished work. Watch for places where a UI button and the server rule disagree; the flow traces point out several.

excerpts.quote: `roleOrder` (`src/lib/auth/permissions.ts:20-24`) maps `VIEWER` to 1, `EDITOR` to 2, and `ADMIN` to 3. `hasMinimumRole` compares the numbers (`:26-28`).
This app is not multi-tenant. Isolation is **author ownership of unpublished work**:

items.title: How much curation can add to a search score
items.body:
The key is right: at most 5.25 points. The ranked SQL adds two curation terms to the text rank: `CASE WHEN "isFeatured" THEN 1.5 ELSE 0 END` and `"manualBoost" * 0.15`. The guide gives the boost's range as 0 to 3.75, which means `manualBoost` goes up to 25. So the most an admin can add is 1.5 (featured) + 3.75 (full boost) = 5.25, on top of whatever `textRank` the words earn.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Exactly 3.75": that is only the boost part, and it is a maximum, not a fixed amount.
- "Unlimited, it multiplies the rank": the boost is *added*, and multiplied only by 0.15.
- "At most 1.5": that is only the featured bonus.

excerpts.quote: "textRank" + CASE WHEN "isFeatured" THEN 1.5 ELSE 0 END + ("manualBoost" * 0.15) ) AS "score",
Answer: `manualBoost x 0.15` (0 to 3.75) plus 1.5 for featured, so at most 5.25 on top of `textRank`.

items.title: A pre-check is a message; the unique index is the guard
items.body:
`createDraftEntry` looks the slug up on the shared client before its transaction opens. When two requests interleave so that both look-ups run first, both see no row and both go on to insert. PostgreSQL's unique index on the slug lets one insert commit and rejects the other, and Prisma reports that as a known request error with code P2002. The route's `apiError` recognises only application errors and zod errors, so the loser gets a logged 500 rather than the 409 the pre-check would have produced a moment later.

The robust pattern is to treat the database constraint as the rule: catch P2002 on the slug and map it to the same 409, keeping the pre-check only for a friendly early answer.

- *409 from the pre-check* needs the first insert to commit before the second look-up.
- Nothing suffixes slugs or maps P2002.

excerpts.quote: const existingEntry = await findEntryBySlug(input.slug); if (existingEntry) { throw new ConflictError("That slug is already in use");

readMore.why: Which errors keep their status and which become 500.

items.title: A window count only exists on rows you return
items.body:
`COUNT(*) OVER()` is evaluated before `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, so every returned row carries the full match count, 12 here. That makes one query enough for pages 1 and 2. The value lives on the rows, though. Page 3 skips all twelve matches, no row comes back, and the mapper's fallback reports 0. The schema bounds page only from below, so the request is accepted.

A client that renders "page 3 of N" from this response would show zero results and zero pages. A separate count query, as the workspace list uses, keeps the total correct for any page; so does clamping the page to the last one before querying.

- *12* is true for pages 1 and 2 only.
- *2* confuses the remainder on page 2 with the total.
- *400* would need an upper bound on page.

items.title: Goal: what Save does to a published entry
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal asks what happens when an editor presses Save while a **published** entry is selected.

The keyed Check answers it: the save path calls `updateMutation.mutateAsync(payload)` whenever an existing entry is selected, which goes to `updateDraftEntry` on the server. That function checks ownership but not status, so the live content changes at once. Review finding 1 in the auth guide says the same: editors can silently rewrite published content.

Why the other checks do not fit this Goal:
- The "Incident Bridge Template is a DRAFT" check answers the curation-409 Goal.
- The "archived entry shows Publish" check answers the Goal about a button the server always rejects.
- The `slugify("SECURITY")` check answers the shared-tag Goal.
None of them is about saving a published entry.

excerpts.quote: if (hasPersistedEntry && entryId) { const updated = await updateMutation.mutateAsync(payload);
**Editors can silently rewrite published content.** `updateDraftEntry` has no status check

items.title: publishedAt means last published, not first
items.body:
The status update writes `publishedAt` on every transition: the current time when the new status is PUBLISHED, otherwise null. Archiving on 1 April cleared it. The admin's restore to DRAFT left it null, and the publish on 1 May set it to that moment. Nothing keeps the original March date on the entry; only the audit row written for that first status change still records when it happened.

This is a data-model choice worth noticing. Search breaks score ties by `publishedAt`, so a republished entry sorts as if it were new, and a UI that labels the column as the first publication date would be wrong. Keeping `firstPublishedAt` separately would preserve both meanings.

- *1 March* would need the column to be written once.
- *null* forgets the second publish.
- *1 April* would need it to track every status change.

excerpts.quote: publishedAt: status === EntryStatus.PUBLISHED ? new Date() : null,

items.title: The fetch wrapper keeps the message and drops the rest
items.body:
The server does its part: a failed parse becomes a 400 whose body carries a code, a generic message and the flattened zod issues, which name the summary field and its minimum. `apiClient` keeps only `payload.error.message` and throws a plain `Error` with it. The status, the code and the issues are gone before the component sees anything, so the form can only print the generic sentence, and it cannot highlight the summary field or tell a 400 from a 409.

A richer client error (status, code and details, as an `ApiError` class) would let the form map issues onto fields.

- *A field message* exists only inside the dropped issues.
- *Request failed* is the fallback when the body has no message; this one has one.
- *Unable to save entry* is for a thrown non-Error.

items.title: A query nobody invalidates refreshes only when it goes stale
items.body:
Creating a draft can create tags, but none of the entry mutations invalidates `["tags"]`; they invalidate the workspace list, the search results and the edited entry. The tag chips were cached when the editor first opened search, and with a 30 s staleTime they are still fresh 10 s later. Mounting the search page again therefore reuses the cached list without a request, and Payments is missing. It appears after the list goes stale and something triggers a refetch, such as a remount or a window focus after 30 s.

The fix is one more line in the create and update hooks: invalidate `["tags"]` on success.

- No mutation touches `["tags"]`.
- A fresh query does not refetch on mount.
- *Server-rendered tags*: the page passes only the session; the chips come from the client query.

readMore.why: What the create hook invalidates on success.

items.title: Where expired sessions are deleted, and which never are
items.body:
The key is right: an expired session is deleted when it is presented, and sessions that are never presented again stay forever. `getSessionFromToken` looks up the token; if the row's `expiresAt` has passed, it deletes the row and returns null. That only happens when someone sends that cookie. A session whose cookie is never used again is never looked up, so it is never deleted. An index on `expiresAt` exists that would support a cleanup job, but there is no such job.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Never deleted, only null returned": the code does delete on access.
- "A nightly job": the guide says none exists.
- "Deleted for every user on any login": login only creates a session; it does not sweep others.

excerpts.quote: Sessions that are never presented again stay in the table. `Session_expiresAt_idx` (`migration.sql:75`) would support a sweep job, but none exists.

items.title: Start here: a knowledge base with roles, drafts and ranked search
items.body:
This app is an internal knowledge base built with Next.js, Prisma and PostgreSQL. Staff write entries; entries move between DRAFT, PUBLISHED and ARCHIVED; anyone signed in can search published ones. There are three roles: VIEWER, EDITOR and ADMIN.

Suggested reading order:

1. `docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md`: thirteen stops through the code, each ending in a check you can answer with the file open.
2. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md`: sessions, roles, ownership, and five senior review findings.
3. `docs/learning/concepts-demonstrated.md`: each concept with where it lives, how it works, and where it falls short.
4. `docs/learning/flow-traces.md`: five flows from a UI click down to Prisma, each followed by Goal/Check exercises.
5. `docs/learning/build-journal.md` for the history behind the design.

Many quizzes in this pack are those Goal/Check exercises: you get a Goal and must pick the evidence that answers it. The wrong options are real checks from *other* exercises, so you need to know what each flow is about, not just recognise file names.

excerpts.quote: There are thirteen stops. Each one ends with a **Check** you can answer with the file open.
Each trace starts at a UI component, goes through a React Query hook and `apiClient` (`src/lib/http/client.ts:1-20`), and ends at Prisma. Exercises follow each flow.

readMore.why: The thirteen-stop reading path through the code.
Sessions, roles, ownership and the senior review findings.

items.title: An entry never conflicts with its own slug
items.body:
**Key: it saves, because the slug lookup leaves out the entry being edited.**

After the ownership lookup, `updateDraftEntry` checks for a slug clash with `findEntryBySlug(input.slug, entryId)`. The repository adds `NOT: { id: excludeId }` when an id is passed, so the entry's own row is skipped. With no other entry using that slug, nothing is found and the update runs in its transaction.

Why the others are wrong:
- *409 That slug is already in use*: that needs a different entry with the same slug.
- *a numeric suffix*: nothing appends suffixes; a real clash is refused.
- *400*: the schema always derives a slug, and an unchanged one is valid.

readMore.why: The checks before the update transaction.

items.title: Goal: the 409 when an admin curates the seeded draft
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal has two parts: which seeded entry, and which line returns the 409 Conflict.

The keyed Check: the seed creates "Incident Bridge Template" with status DRAFT, and `curateEntry` throws `ConflictError("Only published entries can be curated")` when the entry is not PUBLISHED. The admin passes the role checks, so the request gets as far as this status rule. The code's own note explains why: boosting a draft would distort ordering without affecting public search.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The archived-Publish check is also a 409, but for a status change on an archived entry, not curation.
- The `ReactMarkdown` check is about HTML rendering.
- The slug-fallback check is about empty slugs.

excerpts.quote: if (currentEntry.status !== EntryStatus.PUBLISHED) { throw new ConflictError("Only published entries can be curated");

items.title: Goal: what the seeded editor's workspace shows
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal is a prediction from data: log in as the seeded editor and open the workspace; how many entries appear?

The keyed Check reads the seed: the editor authored the two published entries (`seed.ts:76` and `:109`) and the admin authored the draft (`:140`). The workspace list adds `authorId` for non-admins, so the editor sees their own 2 entries, and the admin, who is not scoped, sees all 3.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The `ReactMarkdown` check is about HTML rendering.
- The slug-fallback check is about empty slugs.
- The `slugify("SECURITY")` check is about tags.
None of them counts entries or looks at who authored them.

items.title: The one transition only admins may make
items.body:
The key is right: restoring an archived entry back to a draft. `canTransitionEntry` first requires that the user can edit the entry. Then it has one special case: if the entry is ARCHIVED and the next status is DRAFT, it returns `user.role === "ADMIN"`. Every other allowed move just goes through the shared transition table, which treats editors and admins the same (on entries they may edit).

Why the others are wrong:
- "Publishing an editor's own draft": editors may do this directly; the guide notes there is no review step.
- "Discarding a draft into the archive": DRAFT → ARCHIVED is in the table with no role condition.
- "Archiving a published entry": PUBLISHED → ARCHIVED is also in the table with no role condition.

excerpts.quote: if (entry.status === EntryStatus.ARCHIVED && nextStatus === EntryStatus.DRAFT) { return user.role === "ADMIN"; }
Editors publish their own drafts directly. There is no review or approval step.

items.title: Goal: a single-entry read broader than the list
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal asks you to find a place where opening **one** entry allows more than the list of entries does. That kind of mismatch is worth noticing in any app.

The keyed Check: `findWorkspaceEntryById` uses `OR: [{ status: PUBLISHED }, { authorId }]` for non-admins. So an editor can open any published entry in the workspace detail view, while the workspace list (`listWorkspaceEntries`) only shows their own. The auth guide says the detail view is read-only for those entries.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The `slugify("SECURITY")` check answers the shared-tag Goal.
- The curation-409 check is about curating a draft.
- The `updateMutation` check is about saving a published entry, a write path, not a read.

excerpts.quote: An editor can open any published entry in the workspace detail view, read-only.

items.title: Which audit action stores the whole input
items.body:
The key is right: `knowledgeEntry.curated`. In `curateEntry`, the audit row is written with `metadata: input`: the entire request input (featured flag, boost, notes) goes into the log. The concepts guide asks this exact question and gives this answer.

Why the others are wrong:
- `knowledgeEntry.updated`: the guide says update events record only the slug, not a diff.
- `knowledgeEntry.created` and `knowledgeEntry.statusChanged`: they are written by other service functions with their own, smaller metadata; the guide singles out curation as the one whose metadata is the whole input.

A side note from the same section: nothing in the app reads the audit log yet, so all of these rows are written but never shown.

excerpts.quote: Update events record only the slug, not a diff (`:154-156`).

items.title: Why the title "!!! ???" is rejected
items.body:
The key is right: the derived slug is empty, so the length refine rejects it. With no slug given, the schema's `.transform` sets `slug: slugify(value.title)`. `slugify` turns every run of other characters into a dash and then strips dashes from both ends, so "!!! ???" becomes an empty string. The `.refine` that follows requires `value.slug.length >= 3` and fails with "Title or slug must generate at least 3 characters".

Why the others are wrong:
- "A random 8-character fallback": no such fallback exists.
- "The literal slug !!!-???": slugify strips punctuation.
- "The title min-length check rejects it first": the title must be at least 5 characters, and "!!! ???" is 7 characters including the space, so it passes that check. It fails later, at the slug.

excerpts.quote: .refine((value) => value.slug.length >= 3, { message: "Title or slug must generate at least 3 characters",

items.title: Every keystroke is a new query key
items.body:
The search box writes straight into React state, and that state becomes part of the query key `["knowledge-search", filters]`. Each letter makes a new key, so typing vpn starts three queries. A new key has no cached data, and the hook sets no `placeholderData`, so each one begins with `isLoading` true and the list shows its loading state until the response lands. Keys already fetched within the 30 s staleTime are served from cache, which is why deleting back to an earlier string sends nothing.

The usual fixes are a debounced value in the key (for example 250 ms) and `placeholderData: keepPreviousData`, so old results stay visible while the next ones load.

- *Debounced* and *one shared key* describe code this repo does not have.
- *Previous results kept* needs `placeholderData`.

items.title: Goal: why a viewer can open a result but not the workspace
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal asks for the *two* rules that make the difference: what the entry page requires, and what the workspace page requires.

The keyed Check gives both. The entry page (`entries/[slug]/page.tsx:18-30`) only redirects to login when there is no session, then shows the entry if it is published. The workspace page (`workspace/page.tsx:13-15`) has an extra line: if the role is VIEWER, redirect to `/`. So a viewer passes the first and is turned away by the second.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The slug fallback check answers the empty-slug Goal.
- The archived-Publish check answers the always-rejected-button Goal.
- The `findWorkspaceEntryById` check answers the Goal about a single-entry read broader than the list; it is about editors inside the workspace, not viewers.

excerpts.quote: const session = await getServerSession(); if (!session) { redirect("/login"); }

items.title: What is odd about createAuditLog's default parameter
items.body:
The key is right: callers must always pass a client positionally, so the default is never used. In JavaScript, arguments fill parameters left to right. `createAuditLog(client: DbLike = db, input)` puts the default on the **first** parameter, with a required `input` after it. To give `input` you must also give something in the first slot. So the default `db` can never kick in by omission. The concepts guide calls this out.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Defaults before required parameters are not allowed in TypeScript": TypeScript accepts it; it is just pointless here.
- "Every audit write escapes the transaction": callers pass the transaction as `client`, which is what makes the audit row commit with the change.
- "Opens a new connection per row": the default refers to the shared `db` client; nothing opens connections.

excerpts.quote: export async function createAuditLog(client: DbLike = db, input: CreateAuditLogInput) {
Callers must always pass a client positionally, so the default can never actually be used.
The service passes its `transaction` into `upsertTagsByNames`, `createKnowledgeEntry`, and `createAuditLog`, so all three commit together.

items.title: Why featuredOnly=false becomes true
items.body:
The key is right: `true`, because `Boolean("false")` is true. Query-string values always arrive as text. `z.coerce.boolean()` converts by calling JavaScript's `Boolean(value)`, and every non-empty string is truthy, including the string "false". So `featuredOnly=false` turns the filter **on**. The concepts guide lists this as a weak spot of the validation boundary. The search hook avoids it by sending `featuredOnly` only when it is true.

Why the others are wrong:
- "A validation error": coercion never fails for a string; it just converts.
- "undefined, then the default": the default only applies when the parameter is missing.
- "false, zod parses the word": `z.coerce.boolean()` does not read the word; it only asks whether the string is empty.

items.title: Goal: is entry content rendered as raw HTML?
items.body:
This is a Goal/Check pair from the flow-traces guide: the Goal says what to find, and the Check is the evidence that answers it. The Goal is a security question: if an editor puts HTML (for example a `script` tag) in an entry, does the browser run it?

The keyed Check answers it: the entry page renders content with `ReactMarkdown` and the `remarkGfm` plugin only, and `package.json` has no `rehype-raw` (the plugin that would allow raw HTML). By default react-markdown does not render embedded HTML, which limits XSS (cross-site scripting) from editor-written content.

Why the other checks do not fit:
- The curation-409 check is about curating a draft.
- The `updateMutation` check is about saving a published entry.
- The archived-Publish check is about a button the server rejects.
None of them says anything about how content is displayed.

excerpts.quote: - **Goal:** Find whether entry content is rendered as raw HTML.

items.title: Trim first, then deduplicate
items.body:
**Key: one tag named Runbooks, because names are trimmed before the dedupe.**

`upsertTagsByNames` computes `dedupe(tagNames.map((tag) => tag.trim()))`. Trimming turns both inputs into `"Runbooks"`, and `dedupe` (a `Set`) keeps one. That name gets slug `runbooks`, one upsert runs, and the final `findMany` by slug returns a single tag. (The save schema already trims each tag too.)

Why the others are wrong:
- *Two tags*: the order is trim, then dedupe.
- *spaces kept*: both the schema and the repository trim.
- *unique constraint failure*: only one upsert runs for that slug.

items.title: Where rules live: schemas, services and repositories
items.body:
Requests in this app pass through three kinds of code, each with its own job.

- **Zod schemas** (`src/lib/validation/`) check and also *normalize* input at the boundary. List, field by field, what the save schema changes or derives before a service ever sees the value.
- **Services** (`src/services/knowledgeEntryService.ts`) own the business rules, and they write audit rows.
- **Repositories** (`src/repositories/`) run the queries. Read how each write function receives its database client, including the signature of `createAuditLog`. The search repository uses hand-written SQL for ranking.

The concepts guide is useful because, for every concept, it says where the code **falls short**. Read those lines as a list of real bugs and quirks: they are the raw material for many quizzes. When one mentions a library behaviour (for example how a Zod helper converts a value), test the claim in your head with a concrete input.

excerpts.quote: For each concept: where it lives, how it works here, the risk if it is done badly, where this code falls short, and a **Check**.
**How it works:** Routes pass `session.user` and parsed input. The service decides, opens `db.$transaction`, and returns `mapWorkspaceEntry(...)`. The response never contains a raw Prisma row.

readMore.why: Every concept with its weak spots.

items.title: Concept: the client cache, the wire and the search query
items.body:
The newer questions in this pack leave the permission rules and look at three other layers.

**The browser cache.** Read `src/components/providers/app-providers.tsx` for the client defaults, then every hook in `src/hooks/`. Write down each query key, and for each mutation in `useEntryMutations.ts` the keys it invalidates. Then find, in `search-dashboard.tsx`, exactly what feeds the search hook's key.

**The wire.** Compare the types in `src/types/knowledge.ts` with what `apiOk` and `apiClient` in `src/lib/http/` actually put on and take off the network.

**The SQL.** Read `searchPublishedEntries` in the entry repository slowly, from the tag filter down to the object it returns. Then read the server pages in `src/app/` and the create path in `src/services/knowledgeEntryService.ts`.

items.title: An IN list inside one EXISTS means any, not all
items.body:
All selected tag slugs go into a single `EXISTS` subquery with `slug IN (...)`. That subquery is true as soon as the entry has one matching tag row, so selecting runbooks and security returns entries tagged with either. Each extra chip therefore widens the results.

If the product wants each chip to narrow, as most facet filters do, the condition must require every tag: one `EXISTS` per selected slug, or a grouped subquery whose `HAVING count(DISTINCT slug)` equals the number of chips. It is worth deciding which semantics the UI promises before writing the SQL, because both are one line apart.

- *Both tags* and *exactly these tags* describe AND or equality semantics.
- *The first chip only* misreads the IN list, which takes every selected slug.

items.title: Why PUBLISHED to PUBLISHED passes the transition check
items.body:
The key is right: yes, any same-status move returns true before the transition table is even looked at. `isValidStatusTransition` begins with `if (currentStatus === nextStatus) return true;`. Only when the statuses differ does it consult `allowedTransitions`. And `canTransitionEntry` for the editor's own entry just returns that result. So the request goes through, and the reading path notes a side effect: re-publishing resets `publishedAt`. The concepts guide lists same-status moves under "where it falls short".

Why the others are wrong:
- "Only admins; editors get 403": the special admin-only case is ARCHIVED → DRAFT, not this one.
- "403, editors cannot touch published entries": editors can transition and even edit their own published entries.
- "409, PUBLISHED may only move to ARCHIVED": the table is never reached for a same-status move.
